'''''Euryale ferox''''', commonly known as '''prickly waterlily''',<ref>{{cite book |editor1-last=Lee |editor1-first=Sangtae |editor2-last=Chang |editor2-first=Kae Sun |title=English Names for Korean Native Plants |year=2015 |publisher=[[Korea National Arboretum]] |location=Pocheon |isbn=978-89-97450-98-5 |page=466 |url=http://www.forest.go.kr/kna/special/download/English_Names_for_Korean_Native_Plants.pdf |access-date=7 March 2019 |via=[[Korea Forest Service]]}}</ref> '''makhānā''', or '''Gorgon plant''', is a species of water lily found in southern and eastern Asia, and the only extant member of the genus ''[[Euryale (plant)|Euryale]]''. The edible seeds, called '''fox nuts''' or '''gorgon nuts''', are dried and eaten predominantly in Asia. 

The plant is cultivated for its seeds in lowland [[pond]]s in India, China, and Japan. The Indian state of [[Bihar]] produces 90% of the world's fox nuts.<!--<ref name="Flora of China"/>--> The [[Chinese people|Chinese]] have cultivated the plant for centuries.<!--<ref name="Mabberley1987"/>--> In India, more than 96,000 [[hectare]]s of Bihar were set aside for cultivation of ''Euryale'' in 1990–1991.<!--<ref name=boris/>--> In the northern and western parts of [[India]], the seeds are often roasted or fried like [[popcorn]].<!--<ref name="foodnavigator"/>-->

== Description ==

''Euryale ferox'' grows in freshwater ponds. The [[leaf|leaves]] are large, round and [[peltate]], often more than {{cvt|1|m|ft|0}} across, sometimes to {{cvt|2.7|m|ft|0}} diameter, with a distinctive puckered top. The stalk is at the centre on the underside.<ref name="Flora of China"/><ref>''Gardener's Chronicle'',  Volume 81 (third series) issue 2098 (March 12, 1927) page 127</ref> The leaves are deep green; the leaf veins are purplish. The stems and leaves are covered in sharp [[prickle (botany)|prickle]]s. The [[flower]]s are 5 cm diameter, with violet outer petals and white inner petals; they often pierce through the leaves. The fruit is a spiny capsule 5–10 cm diameter, containing numerous spongy-textured seeds.<ref name="Flora of China"/> It grows in rich soil under water. It does not tolerate shade or cold during the growing season, though when dormant in winter it is not harmed by severe winter cold.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Euryale ferox Foxnut, Euryale PFAF Plant Database |url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Euryale+ferox |access-date=May 30, 2024 |website=pfaf.org}}</ref><ref name="NC Toolbox"/>

== Reproduction and genomics ==
''Euryale ferox'' is capable of [[self-pollination]]. Pollen is released before the flower opens.<ref name = "Povilus et al., 2015">Povilus, R. A., Losada, J. M., & Friedman, W. E. (2015). [https://academic.oup.com/aob/article/115/2/211/92986 "Floral biology and ovule and seed ontogeny of ''Nymphaea thermarum'', a water lily at the brink of extinction with potential as a model system for basal angiosperms."] Annals of Botany, 115(2), 211-226.</ref> The majority of ''Euryale ferox'' flowers are [[Cleistogamy|cleistogamous]], not opening for [[cross-pollination]], though some normally-opening ([[Chasmogamy|chasmogamous]]) flowers do occur.<ref name="Imanishi & Imanishi, 2014">{{cite journal |last1=Imanishi |first1=A. |last2=Imanishi |first2=J. |year=2014 |url=https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/39315121.pdf |title=Seed dormancy and germination traits of an endangered aquatic plant species, ''Euryale ferox'' Salisb.(Nymphaeaceae) |journal=[[Aquatic Botany]] |volume=119 |pages=80–83|doi=10.1016/j.aquabot.2014.08.001 |bibcode=2014AqBot.119...80I }}</ref>

The chromosome count is n = 29. The genome size is 870.42 Mb.<ref name = "Chen et al., 2017">{{cite journal |url=https://academic.oup.com/hr/article-pdf/doi/10.1038/hortres.2017.51/41958119/41438_2017_article_bfhortres201751.pdf |doi=10.1038/hortres.2017.51 |title=Water lilies as emerging models for Darwin's abominable mystery |date=2017 |last1=Chen |first1=Fei |last2=Liu |first2=Xing |last3=Yu |first3=Cuiwei |last4=Chen |first4=Yuchu |last5=Tang |first5=Haibao |last6=Zhang |first6=Liangsheng |journal=Horticulture Research |volume=4 |issue=1 |page=17051 |pmid=28979789 |pmc=5626932 |bibcode=2017HorR....417051C }}</ref> The chloroplast genome is 159930 bp long.<ref name = "Guo, Z., & Min, 2020">{{cite journal |last1=Guo |first1=Z. |last2=Min |first2=J. |year=2020 |doi=10.1080/23802359.2020.1775516 |doi-access=free |title=Characterization the complete chloroplast genome of ''Euryale ferox'' (Nymphaeaceae), an medicinal plant species in China |journal=Mitochondrial DNA Part B |volume=5 |issue=3 |pages=2389–2390|pmid=33457802 |pmc=7782232 }}</ref>

== Cultivation ==

{{further|Mithila Makhana}}

[[File:Foxnut Makhana - Nawada District - Bihar - 1.jpg |thumb |Lightly roasted puffed makhana]]

The seeds<ref name="Goren-Inbar et al., 2014"/> and petioles are used as food.<ref name="Khapudang et al., 2024">{{cite book |last1=Khapudang |first1=Ringshangphi |last2=Loukrakpam |first2=Lanchenbi Chanu |last3=Jadaun |first3=Sadhana |last4=Sharma |first4=Usha |last5=Siddiqui |first5=Saleem |title=Sustainable Food Systems (Volume I) |chapter=Wild Edible and Wetland Plants of Manipur: Their Sustainable Food Usage |publisher=Springer Nature Switzerland |publication-place=Cham |date=2024 |isbn=978-3-031-47121-6 |doi=10.1007/978-3-031-47122-3_6 |pages=107–129}}</ref> In India, more than 96,000 [[hectare]]s of [[Bihar]], where the local variety (and the nuts it produces) is called ''[[Mithila Makhana]]'', were set aside for cultivation of ''Euryale'' in 1990–1991.<ref name=boris>{{cite book |last=Lariushin |first=Boriss |title=Solanaceae family |date=2012 |isbn=978-1478191834 |page=17 |publisher=Boriss Lariushin }}</ref> 
India is the largest global producer of Makhana (fox nut), with over 90% of cultivation concentrated in the floodplain regions of Bihar, particularly in districts like Darbhanga, Madhubani, and Purnia. Makhana has also emerged as a key agri-export commodity, valued for its nutritional profile and [[geographical indication]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Makhana in India: The Ultimate Guide to Cultivation, Nutrition, Grading & Global Demand |url=https://merakisan.com/makhana-in-india/ |website=Merakisan.com |date=2024 |access-date=August 27, 2025 }}</ref><ref name="Flora of China">{{cite web |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200007078 |title=Flora of China: Euryale ferox |website=efloras.org |access-date=29 January 2025}}</ref> In the northern and western parts of [[India]], ''Euryale ferox'' seeds are often roasted or fried like [[popcorn]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.foodnavigator.com/Article/2018/04/25/Are-popped-lotus-seeds-the-next-popcorn# |title=Are popped lotus seeds the next popcorn? |date=April 25, 2018 |publisher=Foodnavigator |accessdate=March 18, 2021}}</ref> In other types of cooking, they form a porridge or pudding called [[kheer]].<ref name="NC Toolbox">{{Cite web |title=Euryale ferox (Foxnut, Gorgon Plant, Makhana, Prickly Water Lily) |website=North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/euryale-ferox/ |access-date=May 30, 2024}}</ref> The seeds are used in [[Cantonese cuisine|Cantonese soup]],<ref>{{cite journal |title=Plants traditionally used to make Cantonese slow-cooked soup in China |year=2018 |journal=Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine |volume=14 |issue=1 |article-number=4 |doi=10.1186/s13002-018-0206-y |pmid=29334976 |pmc=5769313 |first=Yujing |last=Liu |display-authors=et al. |doi-access=free }}</ref> in [[Ayurveda]] preparations, and in [[traditional Chinese medicine]].<ref name="Flora of China"/><!--do not add medical claims here without reliable evidence, see [[WP:MEDRS]] for the rules--> The seeds accumulate any toxic metals present in the water.<ref name="c806">{{cite journal |last1=Rai |first1=U.N. |last2=Tripathi |first2=R.D |last3=Vajpayee |first3=P |last4=Jha |first4=Vidyanath |last5=Ali |first5=M.B |title=Bioaccumulation of toxic metals (Cr, Cd, Pb and Cu) by seeds of Euryale ferox Salisb. (Makhana) |journal=Chemosphere |volume=46 |issue=2 |date=2002 |doi=10.1016/S0045-6535(01)00087-X |pages=267–272}}</ref>

Evidence from [[archaeobotany]] indicates that ''Euryale ferox'' was a frequently collected wild food source during the [[Neolithic]] period in the Yangtze region, with many finds from the sites of [[Kuahuqiao]], [[Hemudu]], and Tianluoshan.<ref name="Fuller2009">{{cite journal |doi=10.1126/science.1166605 |last1=Fuller |first1=D. Q. |last2=Qin |year=2009 |first2=L. |last3=Zheng |first3=Y. |last4=Zhao |first4=Z. |last5=Chen |first5=X. |last6=Hosoya |first6=L.A. |last7=Sun |first7=G.P. |title=The Domestication Process and Domestication Rate in Rice: Spikelet bases from the Lower Yangtze |journal= Science |volume= 323 |issue=5921 |pages= 1607–1610 |url=https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/science.1166605 |pmid=19299619 |bibcode=2009Sci...323.1607F |s2cid=21357179 |display-authors=5|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The earliest recorded use of ''E. ferox'' is from [[Daughters of Jacob Bridge |Gesher Benot Ya'aqov]], Israel, among artifacts of the [[Acheulean|Acheulean culture]] 750–790,000 years ago.<ref name="Goren-Inbar et al., 2014">{{cite journal |last1=Goren-Inbarand |first1=N. |last2=Melamed |first2=Y. |last3=Zohar |first3=I. |last4=Akhilesh |first4=K. |last5=Pappu |first5=S. |title=Beneath Still Waters – Multistage Aquatic Exploitation of Euryale ferox (Salisb.) during the Acheulian |journal=Internet Archaeology |date=2014-10-11 |issue=37 |url=http://intarch.ac.uk/journal/issue37/goren-inbar_toc.html |access-date=16 October 2014 |doi=10.11141/ia.37.1 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Fox nuts have traditionally been harvested by diving without breathing equipment to a depth of {{cvt|2.4|m}} in freshwater ponds. This is arduous, with skin hazards from mud and the plant's thorns. In the 21st century, the National Research Centre for Makhana has pioneered the plant's cultivation in fields flooded to a depth of {{cvt|30|cm}} which makes production and harvesting easier. The area of land devoted to fox nut production has increased to {{cvt|35000|ha}} by 2022. The centre has developed a more productive variety, increasing farm income, and is designing a harvesting machine.<ref name="Gupta 2024">{{cite news |last1=Gupta |first1=Priti |title=The 'superfood' taking over fields in northern India |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crge77e9j19o |access-date=13 August 2024 |work=[[BBC]] |date=13 August 2024}}</ref>

== Taxonomy ==

The species was described by [[Richard Anthony Salisbury]] in 1805. It is a member of the water lily family [[Nymphaeaceae]].<ref name="POWO, 2023"/> It is the type species of its genus.<ref name="Tropicos b">{{cite web |publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden |title=''Euryale'' Salisb. |access-date=December 12, 2024 |url=https://www.tropicos.org/name/40007311}}</ref> 
In 1811, [[Henry Cranke Andrews]] described ''Anneslea spinosa'', now treated as a synonym of ''E. ferox''.<ref>[[Henry Cranke Andrews|Andrews, Henry Cranke]]. "Anneslea spinosa Andrews", ''The botanist's repository'' 10: t. 618 1811.</ref>
In 1853, [[Jules Émile Planchon]] described ''Euryale indica'', now also treated as a synonym.<ref>[[Jules Émile Planchon|Planchon, Jules Émile]]. "Euryale  indica  Planch.", ''[[Annales des Sciences Naturelles Botanique]]'' III, 19: 29 1853.</ref>
The placement in a separate family Euryalaceae [[Jacob Georg Agardh|J.Agardh]], which was proposed by [[Jacob Georg Agardh]] in 1858,<ref name = "Tropicos">{{cite web |publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden |title=Euryalaceae J. Agardh. |access-date=November 22, 2024 |url=https://tropicos.org/name/100353624}}</ref><ref name="Reveal & Chase, 2011"/> has been rejected.<ref name="Reveal & Chase, 2011">{{cite journal|last1=Reveal |first1=J. L. |last2=Chase |first2=M. W. |year=2011 |url=https://phytotaxa.mapress.com/pt/article/download/phytotaxa.19.1.4/21497 |title=APG III: Bibliographical information and synonymy of Magnoliidae |journal=[[Phytotaxa]] |volume=19 |issue=1 |pages=71–134|doi=10.11646/phytotaxa.19.1.4 |bibcode=2011Phytx..19...71R }}</ref><ref name="GBIF">{{cite web |title=Euryalaceae J.Agardh, 1858 |publisher=Global Biodiversity Information Facility |access-date=August 27, 2025 |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/4940207}}</ref> Unlike other water lilies, the [[pollen]] grains of ''Euryale'' have three [[cell nucleus|nuclei]].<ref name="Cronquist 1981">{{cite book |last=Cronquist |first=Arthur |year=1981 |title=An Integrated System of Classification of Flowering Plants |url=https://archive.org/details/integratedsystem0000cron |url-access= registration |location=New York |publisher=Columbia University Press |isbn=978-0-231-03880-5 |page=[https://archive.org/details/integratedsystem0000cron/page/111 111] }}</ref>

The genus is named after a mythical Greek monster, the [[Gorgon]] [[Euryale (Gorgon)|Euryale]].<ref name=boris/> The specific epithet ''ferox'' means fierce or ferocious in Latin.<ref name="NZPCN a">{{cite web |title=''Datura ferox'' |date=n.d. |publisher=New Zealand Plant Conservation Network |access-date=February 2, 2024 |url=https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/datura-ferox/}}</ref> मखाना ("Makhanā") is the [[Hindi]] name for the plant.<ref>{{cite web |title=Makhana, Mākhaṇa, Makhanā: 6 definitions |date=14 October 2018 |url=https://www.wisdomlib.org/definition/makhana |publisher=Wisdom Library |access-date=27 August 2025}}</ref>

== Distribution ==

''Euryale ferox'' is a [[perennial plant]] native to a range from northern India to Taiwan and through China, Korea, and Japan to far eastern Russia.<ref>{{cite web |title=''Euryale ferox'' Salisb. |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:605350-1 |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens Kew |access-date=19 December 2024}}</ref>

In 2022, ''E. ferox'' was recorded as [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in Serbia, probably dispersed from plants grown in botanical gardens by migrating birds.<ref name="Živković et al., 2023">{{cite conference |last1=Živković |first1=M. |last2=Pejčić |first2=L. |last3=Paskaš |first3=N. |last4=Bajić |first4=A. |last5=Šipoš |first5=Š. |last6=Perić |first6=R. |last7=Novakovic |first7=B. |date=February 2023 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/368394784 |title=First recent record of Prickly Waterlily (Euryale ferox) Salisb. (Nymphaeaceae) in freshwaters of Europe |conference=44th International Association for Danube Research Conference, Krems, Austria}}</ref>

== Conservation status ==

The species is classified on the Red List of endangered plants in Japan and given the designation "vulnerable", as it is threatened both by water pollution and by land reclamation there.<ref name="Imanishi & Imanishi, 2014"/><ref name="Kumar et al., 2019">{{cite journal |last1=Kumar |first1=Nitish |last2=Rani |first2=Shweta |last3=Kuamr |first3=Gaurav |last4=Kumari |first4=Swati |last5=Singh |first5=Indu Shekhar |last6=Gautam |first6=S. |last7=Choudhary |first7=Binod Kumar |title=Physiological and biochemical responses of Makhana (Euryale ferox) to gamma irradiation |journal=[[Journal of Biological Physics]] |volume=45 |issue=1 |date=25 October 2018 |pages=1–12 |pmid=30361812 |pmc=6408554 |doi=10.1007/s10867-018-9511-x |doi-access=free }}</ref> It is similarly rated as vulnerable (VU) in South Korea.<ref name="Kim, 2014">{{cite web |editor-last=Kim |editor-first=S. B. |year=2014 |url=http://archive.nationalredlist.org/files/2016/04/Korean-Red-List-of-Threatened-Species-English-compressed-2.pdf |title=Korean red list of threatened species |publisher=National Institute of Biological Resources}}</ref> It is classified as a species of Least Concern (LC) in the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species due to its extensive use and cultivation in China.<ref name="Zhuang, 2011"/> However, a global population decline has been reported.<ref name="Imanishi & Imanishi, 2014"/>
